title: Ethiopian Honey Wine
community: All of Ethiopia — the ancient fermented honey drink
author: Mama Tigist

heritage.origin: Ethiopia — the ancient mead that predates written history
heritage.history: Tej is Ethiopia's most ancient beverage — a fermented honey wine that has been consumed in the Ethiopian highlands for at least 2,000 years and likely much longer. Made from Ethiopian mountain honey and gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) — a bitter hops-like plant endemic to Ethiopia — tej was historically the drink of Ethiopian royalty and is still served at celebrations and in tej houses (tej bets) across the country. The gesho provides bitterness and acts as a natural preservative. Tej ranges from very sweet and mildly alcoholic (new ferment) to dry and strongly alcoholic (fully fermented).

desc: Ethiopian Tej — the ancient fermented honey wine of Ethiopia. Raw honey dissolved in water with gesho twigs (or hops as a substitute), fermented for 2—3 weeks into a lightly alcoholic, slightly bitter, deeply fragrant traditional wine. The drink of Ethiopian royalty and celebration.
longDesc: Tej is Ethiopia's most important traditional beverage — drunk at celebrations, offered to guests as the highest hospitality, and served in tej houses across the country. The traditional fermentation uses gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) — an Ethiopian plant that provides bitterness similar to hops. The result is a honey wine of genuine complexity.
ingredients: 1 kg raw Ethiopian honey (or good quality raw honey)
// No yeast needed — honey's natural wild yeasts drive fermentation
equipment: Large glass or clay fermentation vessel
steps: Dissolve honey in warm (not hot) water.
Ferment at room temperature for 7—14 days.
Continue fermenting 7—14 more days until desired sweetness/alcohol level.
Strain through cloth. Serve in traditional berele (flask-shaped glasses).
chefTips: Raw honey contains wild yeasts on its surface — no commercial yeast needed.
Taste daily — fresh tej (sweet, mild) to older tej (dry, alcoholic) are both valid.
commonMistakes: Using pasteurised honey — kills the wild yeasts.
Too hot water — kills the yeasts.
cookingScience: Honey fermentation is driven by wild Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains and other yeasts naturally present on honey. The honey's high sugar concentration initially inhibits fermentation — dilution with water is what activates the yeasts. Gesho's bitterness (from compounds similar to hops' alpha acids) inhibits bacterial contamination while allowing yeast activity.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian mountain honey from wild beehives — one of Africa's most sustainable honey traditions.
storage: Sealed container — refrigerate after desired fermentation level reached. Keeps weeks to months.
reheating: Not applicable — serve at room temperature.
culturalNote: Tej is the drink of Ethiopian civilization — served at the court of Emperor Haile Selassie, drunk by Sheba's Queen, and today served in tej houses from Addis Ababa to the smallest highland village. The berele flask-shaped glass from which it is drunk is one of the most distinctive objects of Ethiopian material culture.
